ABSTRACT
Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive types of cancer, known for its high mortality rate, as it is often diagnosed at an 
advanced stage. Early diagnosis holds the potential to prolong patients' lifespans and improve treatment success rates. In this 
study, an innovative method is proposed to enhance the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. Computed tomography (CT) images 
were converted into graphs using the Harris Corner Detection Algorithm and analyzed using deep learning models via transfer 
learning. DenseNet121 and InceptionV3 transfer learning models were trained on graph-­based data, and model parameters were 
optimized using the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). Additionally, classification algorithms such as k-­Nearest Neighbors 
(k-­NN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Random Forests (RF) were integrated into the analysis of the extracted features. 
The best results were achieved using the k-­NN classification algorithm on features optimized by WOA, yielding an accuracy of 
92.10% and an F1 score of 92.74%. The study demonstrated that graph-­based transformation enabled more effective modeling 
of spatial relationships, thereby enhancing the performance of deep learning models. WOA offered significant superiority com-
pared to other methods in parameter optimization. This study aims to contribute to the development of a reliable diagnostic 
system that can be integrated into clinical applications. In the future, the use of larger and more diverse datasets, along with 
different graph-­based methods, could enhance the generalizability and performance of the proposed approach. The proposed 
model has the potential to serve as a decision support tool for physicians, particularly in early diagnosis, offering an opportunity 
to improve patients' quality of life.
1   |   Introduction
Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive and lethal types 
of cancer, known for its high mortality rate, increased incidence, 
and usually diagnosed at a late stage. Early diagnosis is critical 
to increase the survival rate of patients [1, 2]. The 5-­year sur-
vival rate is only 8.7%, despite advances in radiotherapy, surgi-
cal methods, and cancer drugs. The subtle and insidious nature 
of pancreatic tumors makes them difficult to detect with tradi-
tional imaging techniques. Surgery and chemotherapy give a 
5-­year survival rate of approximately 31.5%, which occurs only 
in 10%–20% of patients. Due to widespread or regional metas-
tases, 80%–90% of patients do not benefit from treatment [3–5]. 
However, advances in medical imaging and deep learning offer 
promising new ways to improve the accuracy and efficiency of 
pancreatic cancer detection [1, 6–13].

Computed tomography (CT) imaging is the first and most com-
monly used imaging method in examining pancreatic cancer 
[14, 15]. However, manual interpretation of CT images is difficult, 
time-­consuming, and requires significant expertise. It may also 
vary from operator to operator [15]. Recent studies have shown 
that deep learning can be an alternative to traditional methods.
Deep learning techniques offer many advantages, especially in 
processing medical images, and significantly advance diagnostic 
accuracy. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can learn and 
identify features in sets of images. With this feature, deep learning 
has gone beyond traditional image processing. Deep learning can 
potentially increase diagnostic accuracy and reduce human error 
in medical diagnostic processes. When the works done with deep 
learning methods in the literature are examined, it is seen that the 
studies on cancer diagnosis especially exhibit high performance 
[16–18]. Since pancreatic cancer is particularly difficult to detect in 
its early stages, diagnosing this disease with deep learning meth-
ods can help improve patients' quality of life and survival rates.
1.1   |   Related Works
This section includes a comprehensive evaluation of previous 
related studies. In the study by Zavalsiz et al. [19], deep learning 
models were compared to detect pancreatic tumors. This study 
compared a special CNN model with widely used CNN mod-
els such as VGG-­16 and ResNet. The analyses were performed 
with 5968 CT images. Preprocessing stages and data augmen-
tation techniques were used in the study. It was stated that the 
models successfully classified healthy and cancerous images. 
In the study conducted by Kronberg et  al. [20], deep transfer 
learning methods were used to improve the histopathological 
prediction of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). A two-­
communication neural network was used in the preprocessing 
process to transfer inappropriate tissue fragments to a new 
dataset class. The ResNet18 model used in this approach made 
it possible to distinguish PDAC from histopathological images 
accurately. As a result, it was concluded that deep learning mod-
els are effective in diagnosing pancreatic cancer. In the study 
by Zhang et al. [21], an analysis combining radiomics and deep 
learning features was performed to improve the prognostic per-
formance of resectable PDAC. Using CT images obtained from 
two hospitals, the study investigated how radiomics and transfer 
learning features affect prognostic performance. In addition, the 
study included various methods for feature fusion and reduc-
tion. It was concluded that the feature fusion method based on 
risk score in PDAC patients improved the overall survival per-
formance by 40% compared to traditional methods. The study 
conducted by Preuss et al. [22] investigated the use of radiomics 
and deep learning techniques in the personalized treatment of 
pancreatic cancer. The study examined the advances in early 
diagnosis and treatment personalization of pancreatic cancer. 
While features are extracted manually in radiomics methods, 
features are automatically generated in deep learning methods. 
Both methods aim to collect hidden information from medical 
images that traditional radiology methods miss.
Arulmozhi et al. [23] conducted a study examining deep learn-
ing approaches to classify images of pancreatic tumors. The 
study emphasized the importance of computer-­aided design 
(CAD) systems in diagnosing and treating pancreatic cancer 
and examined the effectiveness of deep learning methods. The 
study demonstrated successful results in classifying pancreatic 
tumors with CNN models.
Studies on the early detection of pancreatic cancer are generally 
based on deep learning-­based image processing techniques. 
Litjens et al. [24] highlighted the potential of deep learning in 
medical image analysis and conducted studies on pancreatic 
cancer detection using standard CNN models on CT images. 
However, since these methods work on a pixel-­based approach, 
they are insufficient in modeling the spatial and structural re-
lationships within the images. To address this limitation, our 
study employs a graph-­based transformation method to effec-
tively model the structural details in pancreatic CT images [24].
The use of optimization algorithms has also garnered signifi-
cant attention in recent years. Rana et al. [25] performed hyper-
parameter optimization of deep learning models using genetic 
algorithms (GA). However, it is well-­known that genetic algo-
rithms suffer from slow convergence and a tendency to get stuck 
in local optima during optimization. In contrast, our study uti-
lizes the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA), which has 
demonstrated superior performance in parameter optimization 
due to its fast convergence capability. This study is the first in 
the literature to apply WOA on graph-­based data for pancreatic 
cancer detection [25].
Transfer learning methods are also frequently employed in 
medical image analysis with small datasets. Chen et al. [26, 27] 
achieved an accuracy of 87.45% in pancreatic cancer detec-
tion using pretrained CNN models. However, these models 
worked directly on pixel-­based data and showed limited per-
formance due to unoptimized hyperparameters. In our study, 
DenseNet121 and InceptionV3 transfer learning models were 
combined with graph representations, and their performance 
was enhanced using WOA optimization. The achieved accuracy 
of 92.10% represents a significant improvement compared to ex-
isting methods in the literature [26].
Moreover, traditional classification algorithms used in pan-
creatic cancer detection have been applied in various studies. 
Johnson and Khoshgoftaar [28] utilized machine learning al-
gorithms such as Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Random 
Forests (RF) for the classification of medical images. However, 
these algorithms, working on raw features, tend to exhibit lower 
performance compared to deep learning-­based methods. In our 
study, the features obtained from graph-­based transformations 
were analyzed with classifiers such as k-­NN, SVM, and RF, with 
the highest performance achieved by the DenseNet121 + k-­NN 
combination [28].
In this study, the graphs obtained by representing CT images 
with graphs were analyzed with deep learning models, and the 
presence of pancreatic tumors was classified. CT images were 
converted to graphs using the Harris Detection Algorithm. 
In the study, pancreatic images represented with graphs were 
classified with DenseNet121 and InceptionV3 transfer learning 
models, and the WOA was used to improve the performance 
of the models. In addition, to transfer learning and optimiza-

2   |   Materials and Methods
2.1   |   Data Collection
The “Pancreatic CT Images” dataset on Kaggle contains CT scan 
images of the pancreas. This dataset contains anonymized files 
and has been used in medical imaging research to identify and 
analyze pancreatic diseases. It can also be used to develop and 
test deep learning models in medical diagnostics. The dataset 
used in this study consists of CT images for the detection of pan-
creatic cancer. The dataset was obtained from the Kaggle plat-
form and includes a total of 1411 CT images. The images are 
categorized into tumor and healthy classes. The class distribu-
tion in the dataset is balanced, with approximately 54% tumor 
and 46% healthy images. The resolution of the images has been 
standardized and formatted appropriately for analysis. This 
dataset comprises anonymized data, ensuring compliance with 
ethical guidelines.
Figure 1 shows the distribution of training and testing data in 
the dataset. The first graph shows the number of normal and 
pancreatic tumor images in the training data, and the second 
graph shows the number of normal and pancreatic tumor im-
ages in the test data. There are a total of 1411 images in the data-
set. A total of 412 (225 normal +187 pancreatic tumor) of these 
images were divided as test (29.2%), and 999 (421 normal +578 
pancreatic tumor) were divided as train (70.8%). While 646 (421

2.3   |   Transfer Learning Using Convolutional 
Neural Network Models
Transfer learning is a powerful technique in deep learning, espe-
cially CNN, that accelerates the learning process and improves 
performance by reusing pretrained models. This method allows 
CNN models trained on large datasets to be readapted for smaller 
datasets or different but similar tasks. Transfer learning provides 
significantly successful results, especially in areas with limited 
datasets [30]. The effectiveness of transfer learning is receiving 
increasing attention in the machine learning and deep learning 
communities as it reduces training time and improves perfor-
mance [31]. In this study, DenseNet121 and InceptionV3, two 
CNN submodels, were used.
DenseNet121: This model connects each layer to previous layers 
to enable more efficient use of weights and easier migration of 
gradients. These dense connections improve the model's learn-
ing capacity and performance by increasing the sharing of pa-
rameters. DenseNet121 alleviates the disappearing gradient 
problem, especially with increasing depth, and achieves higher 
accuracy rates with fewer parameters [32]. The success of this 
model has led to its widespread adoption in the deep learning 
community and its use in various tasks such as image classifi-
cation, object detection, and segmentation. Figure 4 shows the 
architecture of the DenseNet121 model.
InceptionV3: It is a third-­generation deep learning model from 
the Inception family that achieves high performance in image 
classification tasks. InceptionV3 extracts richer features by 
increasing the network's depth and breadth, improving the 
model's overall performance. InceptionV3 requires less com-
puting power and memory usage, providing significant ad-
vantages in practical applications [33]. This model is widely 
used in many deep learning tasks due to its high accuracy 
rates and efficiency. Figure  5 shows the architecture of the 
InceptionV3 model.
2.4   |   Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA)
WOA is a meta-­heuristic optimization algorithm developed by 
Mirjalili and Lewis in 2016. WOA was inspired by the hunting 
strategies of humpback whales [35]. This algorithm attracts 
attention with its effectiveness and efficiency, especially in 
solving engineering problems. Figure 6 illustrates the funda-
mental steps and mathematical model of the WOA. The algo-
rithm begins with the random initialization of a population 
of solutions and the selection of the best solution (X*) based 
on their fitness values. As depicted in the figure, the iterative 
process incorporates three main strategies: encircling prey 
(∣A∣ < 1), random search (∣A∣ ≥ 1), and spiral updating of posi-
tions (p ≥ 0.5). During this process, solutions are continuously 
updated, and any solutions that move outside the search space 
are corrected. The best solution is refined at each iteration 
until the stopping criterion is met. Figure  6 systematically 
outlines this algorithmic flow, providing a detailed represen-
tation of the WOA's operation.

3   |   Proposed Model
Figure  7 represents a comprehensive workflow for detecting 
pancreatic tumors. This workflow can be divided into three 
main stages: Data Collection and Data Preparation, Whale 
Optimization and Classification Algorithms with Transfer 
Learning, and Result Interpretation.
In the first stage, a dataset containing CT images of pancreatic 
tumors forms the basic input for subsequent processing and 
analysis steps. In the next step, the Harris Detection Algorithm 
is applied to detect important points (corners) in the images. 
This step is critical to highlight regions of interest that may in-
dicate the presence of tumors. The outputs obtained from the 
Harris Detection Algorithm are converted to graphic format. 
This transformation facilitates the distinction between images 
with and without tumors.
In the second stage, transfer learning is performed using 
CNNs such as DenseNet121 and InceptionV3, previously 
trained on large image datasets. These models are fine-­tuned 
using the pancreatic tumor dataset, and high-­level features 
relevant to tumor detection are extracted. Additionally, the 
WOA is used to optimize the parameters of the models and 
improve their performance. At this stage, three different clas-
sification algorithms, namely k-­NN, RF, and SVM, are finally 
used to analyze the features extracted from CNNs and opti-
mized by WOA.
The results obtained from each classification stage are com-
bined in the final stage, and a final decision is made. Each stage 
increases the reliability of the classification by adding a layer 
to the analysis. This binary classification, divided into “Tumor” 
and “No Tumor,” helps accurately determine the presence of 
pancreatic tumors.

outperforms other studies in the literature in diagnosing pan-
creatic cancer.

5   |   Conclusion
In this study, a novel approach for the detection of pancreatic 
cancer using CT images has been proposed. The methodology 
involves converting CT images into graph-­based representa-
tions through the Harris Algorithm, optimizing the parameters 
of deep learning models with the WOA, and integrating mul-
tiple classifiers such as k-­NN, SVM, and RF. The combination 
of DenseNet121 and k-­NN demonstrated the highest perfor-
mance, achieving 92.10% accuracy, 90.45% sensitivity, 93.50% 
specificity, 92.74% F1-­score, and 0.8437 MCC with a GDR of 
91.93%. These results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed 
method in accurately distinguishing between pancreatic tumor 
and healthy tissues.
The use of graph-­based transformation is particularly sig-
nificant as it enhances the model's ability to capture spatial 
relationships and structural details within the medical im-
ages, which are often overlooked in pixel-­based methods. 
Furthermore, WOA's role in hyperparameter optimization has 
been critical in boosting the performance of transfer learn-
ing models (DenseNet121 and InceptionV3). The inclusion of 
MCC and GDR further provided a balanced evaluation of the 
model's performance, particularly in handling class imbal-
ances inherent in medical datasets.
This study contributes to the existing literature by presenting 
an integrated framework that combines graph-­based repre-
sentation, transfer learning, and metaheuristic optimization 
for pancreatic cancer detection. The proposed method shows 
significant promise as a clinical decision support tool, aiding 
radiologists in the early diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. Early 
diagnosis is crucial for improving patient survival rates and en-
abling timely intervention, as pancreatic cancer is often detected 
at advanced stages with poor prognosis.
In future work, the generalizability of the proposed approach 
can be further enhanced by using larger and more diverse 
datasets collected from multiple sources. Additionally, explor-
ing alternative graph-­based transformation techniques and 
optimization algorithms could further improve performance. 
The integration of ensemble learning methods and real-­time 
clinical validations can also bridge the gap between research 
and practical applications. Overall, the results obtained 
demonstrate the potential of the proposed model as a reliable 
and efficient tool for improving pancreatic cancer diagnosis in 
clinical settings.

Abstract: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive types of cancer, known for its high mortality rate, as it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Early diagnosis holds the potential to prolong patients' lifespans and improve treatment success rates. In this study, an innovative method is proposed to enhance the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. Computed tomography (CT) images were converted into graphs using the Harris Corner Detection Algorithm and analyzed using deep learning models via transfer learning. DenseNet121 and InceptionV3 transfer learning models were trained on graph-­based data, and model parameters were optimized using the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). Additionally, classification algorithms such as k-­Nearest Neighbors (k-­NN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Random Forests (RF) were integrated into the analysis of the extracted features. The best results were achieved using the k-­NN classification algorithm on features optimized by WOA, yielding an accuracy of 92.10% and an F1 score of 92.74%. The study demonstrated that graph-­based transformation enabled more effective modeling of spatial relationships, thereby enhancing the performance of deep learning models. WOA offered significant superiority com- pared to other methods in parameter optimization. This study aims to contribute to the development of a reliable diagnostic system that can be integrated into clinical applications. In the future, the use of larger and more diverse datasets, along with different graph-­based methods, could enhance the generalizability and performance of the proposed approach. The proposed model has the potential to serve as a decision support tool for physicians, particularly in early diagnosis, offering an opportunity to improve patients' quality of life.
